name: Cherokee Buffalo, Hominy and Bean Hot Pot
region: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians / Indigenous Americas
imageAlt: Illustrative USDA photograph of bison meat supplied for tribal food-distribution programs; not a photograph of the finished Cherokee hot pot
imageCredit: Photo: USDA via Wikimedia Commons, U.S. government work. The image illustrates bison as an ingredient and is not presented as a photo of the finished EBCI recipe.
summary: An Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods hot pot of bison, hominy, beans and tomato, adapted directly from a publicly shared Cherokee recipe.
lead: Bison, hominy and beans come together in a straightforward Cherokee hot pot published by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ own Tribal Foods program.
about: This recipe is based on Buffalo, Hominy and Bean Hot Pot published by Tribal Foods, an Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians resource. The original recipe is credited to Watson Harlan and described as a hearty home favorite suitable for beginner cooks. It intentionally uses practical pantry ingredients such as canned hominy, beans and tomatoes alongside bison.
story: The EBCI Tribal Foods project places recipes inside a broader Cherokee foodways effort rather than presenting them as isolated curiosities. Its public recipe describes this hot pot as a home-style meal and explicitly frames canned foods as useful when drained, rinsed and seasoned thoughtfully. That modern practicality belongs to living Cherokee foodways just as much as historical ingredients do; this page therefore follows the community-published recipe instead of inventing an older or more ceremonial origin story.
caveat: This is a home adaptation of a specific recipe publicly shared by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods program. It should not be generalized into a universal Cherokee dish or treated as ceremonial food knowledge.
prepNotes: Drain and rinse canned ingredients
The source recipe specifically notes that canned foods benefit from draining and rinsing so excess canning liquid does not dominate the stew.
Brown bison quickly
Bison is lean. Brown it for flavor, then avoid prolonged hard cooking that can dry it out.
Keep the stew hearty, not soupy
Hominy and beans should remain prominent, with enough tomato-rich liquid to bind the pot rather than flood it.
ingredients: 1 can (15 oz) hominy, drained and rinsed
1 can (15 oz) pinto, kidney or other beans, drained and rinsed
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Drain and rinse the hominy and beans thoroughly. Dice the onion and prepare the bison before heating the pan.
Heat oil in a heavy skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add bison and brown for 4–5 minutes, breaking ground meat into substantial pieces rather than tiny crumbs.
Add onion and cook 2–3 minutes until it begins to soften.
Add tomatoes, hominy and beans. Stir gently and bring to a simmer.
Reduce heat to medium-low and cook 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add a small amount of water only if the mixture threatens to catch on the bottom.
Checkpoint: bison should be cooked through but still juicy, hominy should be tender and the tomato liquid should lightly coat the beans rather than pool around them.
Season with salt and pepper and serve hot.
sources: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Buffalo, Hominy and Bean Hot Pot with Blue Corn Pan Pone
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Cherokee Foodways

name: Sudanese Ta’mia
imageAlt: Sudanese ta’mia falafel patties sold as street food
imageCredit: Photo: Vale287, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons licensed
summary: Sudanese ta’mia made from soaked chickpeas, garlic, coriander and dill, shaped into flat patties and fried until deeply crisp outside and tender within.
lead: Chickpeas, dill and coriander become Sudanese ta’mia—crisp, flat patties with a soft, herb-flecked center.
about: Ta’mia is Sudan’s version of the broad falafel family. Sudanese Kitchen documents a chickpea-based preparation flavored with garlic, coriander and fresh dill and shaped into small flattened patties before frying. Other Sudanese households may use black-eyed peas or other legumes, but this page follows that documented chickpea version.
story: Falafel-like fried legume foods span northeast Africa and the Middle East, but local formulas differ. Sudanese ta’mia is commonly sold as street food and eaten in bread or on its own. The flattened shape, dill and chickpea base distinguish the specific published version used here. Rather than claiming a single origin for falafel as a whole, this page focuses narrowly on how Sudanese cooks make and serve their own ta’mia.
caveat: Legume choice, herbs and shaping vary across Sudanese cooks. This version follows a Sudanese Kitchen chickpea-and-dill formula and should not be read as the only Sudanese ta’mia style.
prepNotes: Use soaked, uncooked chickpeas
Cooking the chickpeas first creates a softer mixture that can fall apart or turn pasty in the oil.
Keep the grind coarse
The mixture should hold together when compressed while still showing tiny chickpea particles.
Add baking powder near frying time
This keeps its lift active instead of letting it sit for hours in the mixture.
ingredients: 2 cups dried chickpeas, soaked 8 hours or overnight and drained
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 to 3 tbsp all-purpose flour, only if needed for binding
steps: Drain soaked chickpeas very well. Pulse them with garlic in a food processor until coarse and evenly ground; do not process into hummus-like puree.
Mix in coriander, dill, cilantro if using and salt. Add water a tablespoon at a time until a compressed spoonful holds together.
Checkpoint: the mixture should feel moist and malleable but not smear like paste. If overly wet, work in flour 1 teaspoon at a time.
Mix in baking powder shortly before frying. Heat oil to about 350°F.
Shape heaping tablespoons into small flat discs, pressing edges together firmly. Press sesame seeds onto the surface if using.
Fry in batches for about 4 minutes total, turning once, until deep golden brown.
Checkpoint: the exterior should be crisp enough to resist gentle pressure while the center remains soft, green-flecked and fully hot.
Drain well and serve warm in bread, with salad or with sauces and pickles.

name: Nigerian Jollof Rice
imageCredit: Photo: Halima Waziri, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Nigerian jollof rice cooked in a reduced red-pepper and tomato stew with thyme, curry spice and long-grain parboiled rice.
lead: Long-grain rice absorbs a smoky red pepper-tomato stew in the Nigerian branch of West Africa’s great jollof family.
about: Jollof is a West African rice tradition with important national styles across the region. Nigerian jollof commonly begins with a blended tomato, red bell pepper and onion base that is cooked down with tomato paste and seasonings before parboiled long-grain rice steams directly in the stew. Party versions often pursue a deeper smoky edge.
story: Food Network’s Nigerian jollof recipe from Nigerian cook Gabi Odebode places the dish inside the wider West African jollof family and notes the Nigerian preference for long-grain parboiled rice and a tomato-red-pepper stew. The dish is central to celebrations, weddings and everyday arguments over whose jollof is best. This page keeps that national specificity while acknowledging the dish’s broader Senegambian and West African history.
caveat: Nigerian jollof varies by region, household and occasion. This is a tomato-and-red-pepper party-style home version, not a claim that Nigerian jollof has one fixed spice blend.
prepNotes: Reduce the pepper base fully
If the blended peppers still smell raw before the rice goes in, the finished jollof will taste thin.
Use parboiled long-grain rice
It holds its shape through the long steam better than many softer rice varieties.
Keep the lid tight
Jollof finishes by steaming in a controlled amount of liquid; escaping steam can leave the top grains undercooked.
ingredients: 4 cups chicken or vegetable stock, approximately
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Blend bell peppers, tomatoes, half the onion, Scotch bonnet and garlic until smooth.
Heat oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Slice the remaining onion and cook 4–5 minutes until softened.
Add tomato paste and fry 3–4 minutes until it darkens slightly and the oil turns red.
Add the blended pepper mixture, thyme, curry powder, paprika and bay leaves. Cook uncovered 15–20 minutes, stirring often.
Checkpoint: the stew should become noticeably darker and thicker, with oil beginning to glisten separately around the edges and no raw-pepper smell.
Stir in rinsed rice until every grain is coated in the red stew. Add enough stock to sit just level with or slightly above the rice.
Bring to a simmer, cover tightly and reduce heat to very low. Steam 30–35 minutes, checking once near the end and adding only a small splash of hot stock if needed.
Checkpoint: rice should be tender and separate with almost all liquid absorbed. For a party-style smoky edge, leave over very low heat another 5 minutes without stirring before fluffing.
Rest covered 10 minutes, remove bay leaves, fluff gently and serve with plantains, salad, meat or fish.
sources: Food Network — Nigerian Jollof Rice by Gabi Odebode

name: Trinidad Doubles
imageAlt: Trinidad doubles with fried bara and curried chickpeas
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons photograph of Trinidad and Tobago doubles, Creative Commons licensed
summary: Trinidad doubles: two soft turmeric bara topped with curried channa and the chutneys, pepper sauce and cucumber that turn it into the island’s signature street food.
lead: Two soft fried bara, warm curried chickpeas and whatever combination of tamarind, pepper and chutney you ask the vendor to pile on top.
about: Doubles is one of Trinidad and Tobago’s most recognizable street foods: two pieces of soft fried bara topped with curried channa and customized with chutneys, pepper sauce and often cucumber. The name and structure are inseparable—one piece of bara is not a double.
story: Tourism Trinidad calls doubles an iconic culinary treat and publishes a full home recipe developed with Foodie Nation. The food emerged from Trinidad’s Indo-Caribbean community and today vendors sell it across the island, from early-morning stands to busy roadside strips such as Debe. Its appeal is partly customization: customers specify how much pepper, tamarind or chutney they want and eat the saucy snack by hand.
caveat: Vendor bara can be exceptionally soft and fast-fried in ways that take repetition to master. This recipe follows Tourism Trinidad’s public home method and scales the frying temperature slightly more conservatively for a household kitchen.
prepNotes: Keep bara dough sticky
Adding enough flour to make it dry and easy to handle produces tougher bread. Oil your hands instead.
Cook channa until saucy
The chickpeas should have enough thick curry liquid to soak the bara without running off completely.
Fry bara very quickly
Thin pieces need seconds, not minutes. Long frying makes them crisp when doubles should remain soft and flexible.
ingredients: 1 tsp instant or active dry yeast
1 cup plus 3 tbsp warm water, approximately
1 tbsp neutral oil for the dough, plus oil for frying
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Tamarind sauce, green chutney, pepper sauce and grated cucumber, for serving
steps: Mix flour, sugar, salt, turmeric and yeast. Add warm water gradually until a very soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead just 1–2 minutes, rub the surface with oil, cover and rest about 30 minutes.
For the channa, combine chickpeas, water, garlic, salt and curry powder in a saucepan. Bring to a boil and cook uncovered 10 minutes.
Add cumin and culantro and cook another 5–10 minutes, lightly crushing some chickpeas. Checkpoint: the mixture should be saucy and spoonable rather than dry.
Heat 1 to 1 1/2 inches frying oil to about 375°F. Oil your hands and work surface.
Pinch off golf-ball-size dough pieces and stretch each into a very thin 4- to 5-inch oval.
Fry one bara at a time for roughly 10–20 seconds per side, just until puffed and cooked without becoming crisp or deeply browned.
Checkpoint: finished bara should fold easily around filling and remain tender after draining.
For each serving overlap two bara, spoon hot channa over them and finish with tamarind, green chutney, pepper sauce and cucumber to taste.
sources: Tourism Trinidad — Street Food Favourites: How to Make Trini Doubles
Tourism Trinidad — Indo-Trinidadian Food and Singh’s Doubles

name: Azerbaijani Suzme Plov
imageAlt: Azerbaijani plov with rice and accompaniments
imageCredit: Photo: Urek Meniashvili, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
summary: Azerbaijani suzme plov with partially boiled saffron rice steamed over a crisp lavash crust and served with lamb, chestnuts and dried fruit.
lead: Saffron rice is parboiled, drained and steamed over crisp lavash while lamb, chestnuts and dried fruit cook separately for the Azerbaijani table.
about: Azerbaijan has many plov traditions. Suzme plov is the drained-and-steamed style: rice is partially boiled in abundant salted water, drained, enriched with butter and saffron and then steamed slowly. A crisp crust called qazmaq forms at the bottom, often from lavash, while meat and fruit may be prepared separately and served with the rice rather than stirred through it.
story: Azerbaijan’s official tourism site calls plov one of the crowning dishes of Azerbaijani cuisine and distinguishes dashma, suzme and dosheme methods. Its published suzme recipe specifically describes partially cooked rice drained and steamed over flatbread, saffron poured over the rice and a separate lamb accompaniment with chestnuts, dried apricots, plums and onions. The separation of rice from garnish is one of the features that distinguishes many Azerbaijani plovs from mixed pilafs.
caveat: Azerbaijan.travel notes more than three major methods and many named plovs. This page follows its suzme-style structure and does not imply that all Azerbaijani plov uses the same garnish or crust.
prepNotes: Rinse and soak the rice
Long, separate grains are the goal; rinsing and a short soak help the rice survive parboiling and steaming.
Parboil only partway
Rice should bend but retain a firm center when drained; fully cooking it before steaming leads to mush.
Protect the steam
Wrap the lid with a clean towel so condensation does not drip back onto the rice.
ingredients: 3 cups basmati or other long-grain rice
2 tbsp kosher salt for the boiling water
1/4 tsp saffron threads bloomed in 1/4 cup hot water
1 lb lamb shoulder, cut into bite-size pieces
Salt and black pepper to taste
steps: Rinse rice until the water is mostly clear, then soak it in cool salted water for 30 minutes and drain.
Bring a large pot of generously salted water to a boil. Add rice and boil 5–7 minutes.
Checkpoint: a grain should be flexible outside but still distinctly firm in the center. Drain immediately and rinse briefly with warm water.
Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a heavy pot. Line the bottom with lavash, trimming or overlapping as needed to cover it completely.
Mound the parboiled rice loosely over the lavash, drizzle with 2 tablespoons melted butter and most of the saffron water. Wrap the lid in a clean towel and cover tightly.
Steam over the lowest heat 35–45 minutes. Do not stir.
Meanwhile brown lamb in the remaining butter, add onions and cook until soft, then add chestnuts, apricots, plums and raisins with a splash of water. Cover and simmer until lamb is tender.
Checkpoint: rice grains should be long, separate and fully tender, while the lavash underneath is crisp and deeply golden.
Turn rice onto a platter, break the qazmaq into pieces and arrange around it. Spoon the lamb-and-fruit accompaniment separately or alongside, not mixed through the rice.
sources: Fringe Table — Caucasus, Central & West Asia food guide

name: Sri Lankan Parippu Curry
imageCredit: Photo: Varghesepunnamada, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licensed
summary: Sri Lankan red lentil parippu simmered with turmeric and coconut milk, then finished with a sizzling temper of mustard seed, curry leaf, onion and dried chile.
lead: Creamy red lentils meet coconut milk and a crackling curry-leaf temper in one of Sri Lanka’s most everyday curries.
about: Parippu is Sri Lankan dhal curry, usually made from red lentils cooked until creamy with turmeric and coconut milk. A separate tempering of mustard seed, curry leaves, onion, garlic and dried chile adds fragrance and textural contrast. It can accompany rice and curry, string hoppers, roti, bread and many other meals.
story: Sri Lanka Tourism describes dhal as one of the country’s most commonly consumed staple dishes and notes that it appears in milky, spicy and tempered forms, usually from red masoor lentils cooked with spices and coconut milk. The finishing temper is a defining household technique: hot flavored oil is poured or stirred into soft lentils at the end, giving an inexpensive everyday dish a fresh burst of aroma.
caveat: Sri Lankan parippu ranges from loose and milky to thick and strongly tempered. This version uses coconut milk and a final temper; households differ in fenugreek, pandan, cinnamon, chile and curry-powder use.
prepNotes: Rinse red lentils well
Removing excess surface starch keeps the curry creamy rather than gluey.
Do not hard-boil coconut milk
Once coconut milk goes in, use gentle heat to keep the texture smooth.
Temper until aromatic, not burnt
Mustard seeds should pop and curry leaves should crackle, while onion turns golden rather than dark brown.
ingredients: 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 small red onion or 3 shallots, thinly sliced
steps: Combine rinsed lentils, water, turmeric, salt, green chile and cinnamon if using. Bring to a simmer and cook 15–18 minutes until the lentils collapse easily.
Stir in coconut milk and reduce heat to low. Simmer gently 4–5 minutes.
Checkpoint: the dhal should be creamy and pourable, with almost no firm lentil centers remaining. Add hot water if it has become stiff.
Heat oil in a small skillet. Add mustard seeds and cover loosely until they begin popping.
Add fenugreek, curry leaves, onion, garlic and dried chile. Fry 3–5 minutes until onion edges are golden and the curry leaves smell toasted.
Immediately scrape the entire hot tempering into the dhal and stir once or twice.
Taste for salt and serve with rice, string hoppers, roti or other Sri Lankan curries.
shop: Sri Lankan red lentils masoor dal
sources: Sri Lanka Tourism — Culinary Tourism: Dhal

name: Northern Thai Khao Soi Gai
region: Northern Thailand / Chiang Mai / Southeast Asia
imageAlt: Chicken khao soi in Chiang Mai with fried noodles and traditional condiments
imageCredit: Photo: Takeaway, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
summary: Chiang Mai-style chicken khao soi with egg noodles in a coconut curry broth, topped with crisp noodles and served with pickled mustard greens, shallot and lime.
lead: Soft egg noodles in fragrant coconut curry, crowned with crisp noodles and sharpened at the table with pickles, shallot and lime.
about: Khao soi is one of Northern Thailand’s signature noodle dishes and is especially associated with Chiang Mai. The familiar northern Thai form combines egg noodles with chicken, beef or pork in a coconut-milk curry broth, then contrasts the soft noodles with a nest of fried crisp noodles and condiments including pickled mustard greens, shallot, lime and chile oil.
story: The Tourism Authority of Thailand describes khao soi as a standard and representative Northern Thai curry noodle dish, built from egg noodles and a mild coconut-milk curry with tender meat. The dish also reflects northern Thailand’s long connections with neighboring Myanmar and Muslim trading communities, and historical narratives around its development vary. Rather than choosing one disputed origin story, this page focuses on the Chiang Mai preparation and its characteristic combination of curry broth, two noodle textures and sharp condiments.
caveat: Khao soi has regional relatives and multiple origin narratives. This is specifically a Chiang Mai-style chicken version, not the Lao khao soi noodle dish and not a claim to represent every northern Thai community.
prepNotes: Use real egg noodles
Fresh Chinese-style egg noodles give the characteristic springy texture and can be split between boiled and fried portions.
Fry the curry paste in coconut cream
Letting the thick coconut cream release some oil helps the paste become fragrant instead of tasting raw.
Serve condiments separately
Pickled mustard greens, shallot, lime and chile oil are part of the eating experience and let each bowl be balanced at the table.
ingredients: 2 tbsp neutral oil, plus more for frying noodles
1/3 cup northern Thai or red curry paste
1 can (13.5 oz) full-fat coconut milk, thick cream and thin milk separated if possible
2 lb bone-in chicken thighs or drumsticks
2 tbsp fish sauce, plus more to taste
steps: Reserve about one quarter of the noodles for frying. Separate the remaining noodles into four portions for boiling later.
Heat 2 tablespoons oil and the thick coconut cream in a pot over medium heat. Cook until bubbling vigorously, then add curry paste, curry powder and turmeric.
Fry 3–5 minutes until intensely fragrant and small beads of colored oil appear around the paste.
Add chicken and turn to coat. Add remaining coconut milk and stock and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add fish sauce and sugar. Simmer 35–45 minutes until chicken is tender and reaches at least 165°F near the bone.
Checkpoint: broth should be rich but pourable, savory and aromatic with coconut supporting rather than muting the curry. Adjust fish sauce or sugar carefully.
Meanwhile fry the reserved noodles in 350°F oil in small nests until crisp and golden; drain well.
Boil the remaining fresh noodles until just tender, drain and divide among bowls.
Ladle chicken and curry broth over the soft noodles and crown each bowl with crisp noodles. Serve pickled mustard greens, shallot, lime and chile oil alongside.
sources: Tourism Authority of Thailand — Khao Soi
